$comment: T-3578 format, the smooth style (T-3696; docs/AUDIO.md § Narration style): the same words as the panel shows, with ElevenLabs v3 audio tags in square brackets and [short pause]/[long pause] and ellipses for pauses, a pause at each change of subject, no whispering, at most one laugh. Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Chicago's First Murder.

[short pause] Chicago in 1812 is a diminutive, congested frontier community: a garrison of about fifty soldiers under Captain Nathan Heald, a government trading house, and a few houses on the north bank. [short pause] Everyone is acquainted with everyone, and the two men who will confront each other at the gate have been antagonists for years, contesting a house, the soldiers' commerce, and the appropriate treatment of their neighbors as war with Britain approaches.

[short pause] Nine stops: the killing initially, then the narrative from 1804 to the night of the killing and the morning after, with the time of day and the season set for each. [short pause] Three competing versions are presented simultaneously: the Kinzie family's, perpetuated for a century; the testimony of a girl who observed from inside the fort; and the correspondence the factor and the surgeon's mate sent to Washington within weeks.

[short pause] The narrative commences at its conclusion: outside the gate of Fort Dearborn, at sunset on 17 June 1812.
scripts.stop:cold-open: [gravely] 17 June 1812, sunset, outside the gate of Fort Dearborn. [short pause] Jean Lalime, the fort's interpreter, lies dead in the dust. The man walking away, bleeding from the shoulder, is John Kinzie, the trader who supplies the garrison, whom later histories would call "The Father of Chicago". [short pause] The perpetrator's identity has never been seriously disputed; his motive, and whether the act constituted murder, depends entirely upon whose testimony you credit. [short pause] To comprehend how events reached this point, travel back eight years, across the river, to the finest house in Chicago.
scripts.stop:du-sable-house: [measured] Eight years earlier. [short pause] May 1804, morning. This is the finest house in Chicago, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, the trader who settled here first. [short pause] In 1800 he sold out, and the deed recorded in Detroit names the buyer as Jean Lalime, a French interpreter and trader, using money from their shared employer, the fur trader William Burnett. [short pause] The witness who signed it was John Kinzie, another of Burnett's traders. Now Kinzie relocates his family here and appropriates the property, although no documentation of any sale from Lalime to Kinzie has ever been found. [short pause] The family later insisted Kinzie bought the place from a "Le Mai", and historians long treated "Lalime" as a misspelling. [short pause] Lalime did not depart; he relocated a few doors west, sufficiently close to observe Kinzie occupying his house, a perpetual reminder of the grievance.
scripts.stop:lalime-house: [measured] Seven years later. [short pause] 26 May 1811, afternoon. Lalime had wintered in the big house in 1803 and 1804 with the fort's first surgeon, who called him "a very decent man and a good companion". [short pause] When Kinzie took possession, Lalime moved here, to a smaller house west along the bank, and became the fort's interpreter, the man who speaks for the garrison with its neighbors. [short pause] Today he writes to Governor William Clark at St. Louis that "An Indian from the Peorias passed here yesterday" with word of horses stolen from the southern settlements. His letters reveal, Kirkland wrote, "a man of ability and education". [short pause] Across the river, a new commercial arrangement is about to enrich Kinzie considerably, and transform Lalime into his adversary.
scripts.stop:factory: [measured] Nine months later. [short pause] 10 March 1812, morning, at the factory, the government's own trading house, operated at cost by the factor, Matthew Irwin. The sutler is something different: a private merchant licensed to sell to the soldiers. In January Captain Heald made "Messrs. [short pause] Kinzie & Forsyth", Kinzie's trading firm, the garrison's exclusive sutlers, and today Irwin informs Washington that the pair had offered someone "400$ per annum" to secure them the post. [short pause] Two men side with Irwin: the young surgeon's mate, Isaac Van Voorhis, and the interpreter, Lalime. Kinzie, an older officer once wrote, was "a man of ungovernable temper". [short pause] Within weeks, a financial dispute escalates into open discussion of killing.
scripts.stop:bad-blood: [measured] Five weeks later. [short pause] 16 April 1812, the officers' barracks. Ten days ago men "supposed to be Winnebagoes" killed two farmhands at Hardscrabble, up the South Branch, and generalized fear has turned residents against one another. [short pause] Irwin writes today that "Propositions were openly made to murder" neighbors who had always been peaceable, French settlers among them, and he identifies who pressed hardest: "the Suttler for this garrison & his Son-in law—Lt Helm", meaning Kinzie and Lieutenant Linai Helm, the fort's second officer, married to Kinzie's stepdaughter. [short pause] Ensign George Ronan, the youngest officer, threatens to shoot Lalime, and Helm swears violent revenge against the factor. In May, Heald arrests Helm for plotting to kill six Sauk men who had come in peace, then releases him. [short pause] By June every resident of the fort has aligned with one faction or the other.
scripts.stop:the-quarrel: [measured] Two months later. [short pause] 17 June 1812, about six in the evening, inside the fort. Tomorrow, in Washington, Congress will declare war on Britain, although the news will not reach this isolated garrison until the middle of July. [short pause] On the parade Helm denounces the factor, concluding, as Van Voorhis recorded, "by saying he would give a very handsome treat if the Factory would be done away!" [short pause] Kinzie supports his son-in-law, while Lalime defends Irwin's establishment, having "defended the pure motives and just dealings of the Institution". [short pause] As the confrontation intensifies, Kinzie and Lalime proceed out of the gate together, immediately before the gates close for the night, and only one of the two men will return.
scripts.stop:the-gate: [gravely] An hour later. [short pause] 17 June, sunset, back outside the main gate. Victoire Porthier, a girl inside the fort, recalled decades afterward: "It was sunset, when they used to shut the gates of the fort". [short pause] She heard Helm warn Kinzie to look out for Lalime, "as he had a pistol", and then: "We heard the pistol go off and saw the smoke. Then they fell down together". Kinzie rose, wounded in the shoulder; Lalime did not. [short pause] Irwin, the factor, witnessed everything from twenty or thirty yards, and Van Voorhis insisted that "it was a perfect assassination and can be proven to be such", whereas the Kinzie family characterized it as self-defense. [short pause] With the perpetrator simultaneously the commander's sutler and the lieutenant's father-in-law, the officers must determine how to proceed.
scripts.stop:the-flight: [measured] Four hours later. [short pause] 17 June, about 11:20 at night. According to Irwin, Ensign Ronan told Kinzie to flee, and Helm concealed him in the garrison for about four hours, then walked him to the river's edge, shook his hand and released him. [short pause] According to the family, Kinzie "returned to the house covered with blood", and his wife took him into the woods, where "she dressed his wounds" and kept him hidden for days. [short pause] According to Porthier, "In the night he packed up some things and my father took him to Milwaukee". [short pause] These constitute three irreconcilable versions of a single night, while at the gate, Lalime's body still lies where it fell.
scripts.stop:the-grave: [solemnly] Nine hours later. [short pause] 18 June, morning. The townspeople want an inquest, a public inquiry into the death, but Irwin wrote that instead "a file of soldiers headed by Lt. Helm carried it away by force". [short pause] Lalime was buried on this bank, about "two hundred yards west of the Kinzie house", inside a picket fence, in plain view of the house he had once owned on paper. [short pause] In 1891 workers digging a cellar near Cass and Illinois streets discovered a skeleton in "a rude pine coffin", and the bones were transferred to the Chicago Historical Society.
scripts.ending:verdict:
[measured] That night Heald ordered the factor to assist in arresting Kinzie; Irwin refused and was expelled from the garrison, and Heald's own letter explains the refusal: "a Citizen who had but a few days previous stabed an other citizen to the heart in your presence". [short pause] Irwin departed on 5 July and was captured at Mackinac, Van Voorhis perished on the lake shore on 15 August, and Kinzie survived, returned in 1816, and allowed his family to control the narrative for a century.

[short pause] Was it, then, murder? Historians continue to disagree, and vehemently.

[short pause] THE CASE AGAINST KINZIE. Irwin, writing after the fall of the fort, accused him of helping precipitate the disaster of 15 August, thereby "destroying the Witnesses to the murder of Lalime". [short pause] Milo Quaife, who discovered Irwin's correspondence, warned in 1915 that readers who regarded Kinzie "as a kind of demigod" would experience that accusation as "a distinct shock", and the Chicago Reader in 2018 denounced the self-defense explanation as "a popular lie".

[short pause] THE CASE FOR KINZIE. In the family's interpretation, Lalime, "insanely jealous over Kinzie's success as a trader, treacherously attacked him", and Currey (1912) reports an officers' inquiry reaching "a verdict of justifiable homicide". [short pause] Porthier testified, "You see Kinzie wasn't to blame at all", before adding, revealingly, "That is what they all said".

[short pause] WHO TOLD IT. Quaife observed that exclusively the version "originating with the relatives and friends of the slayer gained the public ear", a reminder that historical memory frequently belongs to the survivors. [short pause] Lalime's remains are still preserved in a box in the Chicago History Museum's storage. [short pause] You have stood where he fell, so evaluate the evidence and decide for yourself.
